title: Boolean Algebra
goal: Switch between logic and `+ · ′` notation, know what makes a Boolean algebra (bits, bit vectors, power sets), and simplify expressions with the laws.
magic: A Boolean algebra: `0`, `1`, `+`, `·`, `′` with commutative, associative, distributive (both ways!), identity and complement laws.
Finite BA ⇒ `2ᵏ` elements ⇒ a copy of `Bᵏ` (subsets = bit vectors).
Shortcuts: `x + xy = x`, `xy + xy′ = x`, `x + x′y = x + y`.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
A formula is a function from bits to a bit
blocks.summary: Plug 0/1 into the letters, get 0/1 out. With `n` letters there are `2^(2ⁿ)` possible functions.
blocks.picture: A light controlled by two switches is a machine: switch settings go in (0/1, 0/1), light on/off comes out. Every such wiring is a Boolean function.
blocks.official: Formulas can be seen as **Boolean functions** mapping each valuation of their letters to `0` (false) or `1` (true): `{0, 1}ⁿ → {0, 1}` (Week 2, slide 44). One input: **unary**; two: **binary**; `n`: **`n`-ary**. The table of the function is the truth table. There are `2^(2ⁿ)` Boolean functions of `n` variables (slide 73: their collection is `bool(n)`).

tries.q: How many different **unary** Boolean functions are there? Name them.
tries.why: `2^(2¹) = 4`: two inputs, each sent to 0 or 1.

tries.q: How many **binary** Boolean functions are there?
tries.why: 4 input pairs, each sent to 0 or 1: `2⁴ = 16`. `∧`, `∨`, `⇒`, `⇔`, `⊕`, nand, … are 6 of them.

tries.q: How many Boolean functions of 3 variables?
As a function, what does `A ∨ ¬A` do?
tries.why: It's a tautology, so the function is the constant 1 (a lecture example, slide 44).

trap.tempting: There are `2ⁿ` Boolean functions of `n` variables.
trap.correct: `2ⁿ` is the number of **rows** (inputs). Each row can output 0 or 1 independently, so there are `2^(2ⁿ)` functions.
trap.test: `n = 1`: 2 rows, but 4 functions. Check your formula on that.

blocks.title: Boolean-algebra notation: `+` is OR, `·` is AND, `′` is NOT
blocks.summary: Same logic, new symbols: `p ∧ q` → `pq`, `p ∨ q` → `p + q`, `¬p` → `p′`. And `1 + 1 = 1`.
blocks.picture: Like switching from Java's `&&`, `||`, `!` to Python's `and`, `or`, `not`: nothing changes except the spelling.
blocks.official: Boolean algebra (BA) notation (Week 2, slides 45 and 53): atoms stay `p, q, …`; `p ∧ q` → `p · q` or `pq`; `p ∨ q` → `p + q`; `¬p` → `p′` (engineers write `p̄`). Values are `0` and `1`, and `+` saturates: `1 + 1 = 1`. Lecture example: `(¬A ∨ ¬B) ∧ B` ↦ `(a′ + b′) · b`. Using `·` saves brackets: `′` binds tightest, then `·`, then `+`.

tries.q: Translate `a ∧ (b ∨ ¬c)` into BA notation.
tries.why: `∧` → juxtaposition, `∨` → `+`, `¬c` → `c′`.

tries.q: Translate `x′ + yz` back into logic notation.
tries.why: `·` binds tighter than `+`, so `yz` is one block.

tries.q: In BA, what is `1 + 1`? And `1 · 0 + 1`?
tries.why: `+` is OR, not arithmetic: T ∨ T = T. `1 · 0 = 0`, then `0 + 1 = 1`.

tries.q: Does `pq′` mean `p · (q′)` or `(pq)′`?
tries.why: `′` binds tightest. For "not (p and q)" write `(pq)′`.

trap.correct: `′` sticks to the single thing right before it: `pq′ = p · q′`. Use brackets for `(pq)′`.
trap.test: Test with `p = 1, q = 1`: `p · q′ = 0`, but `(pq)′ = 0` too. Try `p = 0, q = 0`: `p · q′ = 0`, `(pq)′ = 1`. Different.

blocks.title: A Boolean algebra: `0`, `1`, `+`, `·`, `′` and five pairs of laws
blocks.summary: Any set with a `0`, a `1`, join `+`, meet `·` and complement `′` that obeys the laws. Bits, bit vectors and power sets all qualify.
blocks.picture: Sets with union/intersection, bitmasks with OR/AND, and true/false with `∨`/`∧` all follow the same rules. A Boolean algebra is the name for "anything that follows those rules".
blocks.official: A structure with a set `T` containing `0` and `1`, **join** `x + y`, **meet** `x · y`, **complement** `x′`, is a **Boolean algebra** if for all `x, y, z` (Week 2, slide 47): commutative `x + y = y + x`, `x · y = y · x`; associative; distributive `x + (y · z) = (x + y) · (x + z)` and `x · (y + z) = (x · y) + (x · z)`; identity `x + 0 = x`, `x · 1 = x`; complementation `x + x′ = 1`, `x · x′ = 0`. Examples: 2-bit vectors `B × B` with bitwise operations, `0 = (0, 0)`, `1 = (1, 1)` (slide 48); `Pow(S)` with `∪`, `∩`, `S \ X`, `0 = ∅`, `1 = S` (slide 50).

watch.q: In `Pow({a, b, c})`, compute `{a, b} + {b, c}`, `{a, b} · {b, c}` and `{a}′`.
steps: Join is `∪`: `{a, b} ∪ {b, c} = {a, b, c}` (that's `1`).

tries.q: In `B × B` (2-bit vectors), compute `(1, 0) + (0, 1)` and `(1, 0) · (1, 1)`.
tries.why: Work bit by bit: OR for `+`, AND for `·`.

check.expr: tuple(a | b for a, b in zip((1,0),(0,1)))
tuple(a & b for a, b in zip((1,0),(1,1)))

tries.q: Bit vectors of length 4: compute `(1, 0, 1, 1) · (0, 1, 1, 0)` and `(1, 0, 1, 1)′`.
tries.why: Bitwise AND, then bitwise NOT. (Like `0b1011 & 0b0110` and `~` on 4 bits.)

check.expr: tuple(a & b for a, b in zip((1,0,1,1),(0,1,1,0)))

tries.q: In `Pow({1, 2, 3, 4})`, what are `0` and `1`?
tries.why: `0` is the "nothing" element (`X ∪ ∅ = X`), `1` the "everything" element (`X ∩ S = X`).

tries.q: Check the odd-looking distributive law `x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)` for `x = 0, y = 1, z = 1` in `{0, 1}`. Does it hold in ordinary arithmetic?
tries.a: **In BA: both sides are 1.** In ordinary arithmetic it fails, e.g. `x = y = z = 1`: `1 + 1 = 2` but `(2)(2) = 4`.
tries.why: This second distributive law is special to Boolean algebra.

trap.tempting: `+` and `·` behave exactly like school arithmetic.
trap.correct: They share many laws, but BA also has `x + x = x`, `1 + 1 = 1` and `x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)`, which are false for numbers.
trap.test: If a step would give a 2, you've slipped back into arithmetic.

blocks.magic: Five law pairs; examples: `{0, 1}`, bit vectors, power sets.

blocks.title: Every finite BA has `2ᵏ` elements, and same size means same structure
blocks.summary: A finite Boolean algebra has 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … elements, and all BAs of one size are copies of `Bᵏ`.
blocks.picture: Subsets of `{a, b, c}` and 3-bit masks are the same thing in disguise: `{a, c}` is just `101`. That's why Redis bitmaps and bitsets can do set operations with OR and AND.
blocks.official: **Fact** (Week 2, slide 74): every finite Boolean algebra has `|T| = 2ᵏ` for some `k`. Two BAs are **isomorphic** (`≃`) if a one-to-one correspondence `ι` maps `0 ↦ 0`, `1 ↦ 1` and respects `+`, `·`, `′`. **All** BAs with the same number of elements are isomorphic (slide 75): `n-tuples ≃ Bⁿ`, `Pow(S) ≃ B^|S|`, `Map(S, B) ≃ B^|S|`, `bool(n) ≃ B^(2ⁿ)`. Example: encoding subsets as bit vectors.

watch.q: Encode subsets of `S = {a, b, c}` as bit vectors `(a?, b?, c?)`. Encode `{a, c}` and `{b, c}`, then check that `∪` becomes `+`.
watch.answer: The encoding turns `∪` into bitwise OR (and `∩` into AND, complement into NOT): `Pow(S) ≃ B³`.

tries.q: Can a Boolean algebra have exactly 6 elements?
tries.why: Finite BAs have `2ᵏ` elements: 1, 2, 4, 8, … and 6 isn't a power of 2.

check.expr: 6 not in [2**k for k in range(10)]

tries.q: How many elements does `Map(S, B)` have if `|S| = 5`?
tries.why: Each of the 5 elements of `S` is sent to 0 or 1: `2⁵`.

tries.q: With the encoding `(a?, b?, c?)`, which subset is `(0, 1, 0)′`?
tries.why: Complement flips every bit; in sets, it takes everything **not** in `{b}`.

tries.q: `bool(2)` (all binary Boolean functions) is isomorphic to `Bᵏ` for which `k`?
tries.why: `bool(n) ≃ B^(2ⁿ)`, and `2² = 4`.

trap.tempting: Any finite set with OR/AND-like operations can be a Boolean algebra.
trap.correct: Its size must be a power of 2, and all five law pairs must hold.
trap.test: Count the elements first. Not a power of 2 → not a BA.

blocks.magic: Finite BA ⇒ `2ᵏ` elements ⇒ it's a copy of `Bᵏ`.

blocks.title: Calculating with the BA laws
blocks.summary: Use the laws like algebra rules. The shortcuts that save the most time: absorption and combining opposites.
blocks.picture: Tidying a messy SQL `WHERE` clause: `(a AND b) OR a` is just `a`. BA laws are the rules that make that tidy-up safe.
blocks.official: Useful laws (Week 2, slide 54): `x + x = x`, `xx = x`; `xx′ = 0`, `x + x′ = 1`; `x · 0 = 0`, `x · 1 = x`, `x + 0 = x`, `x + 1 = 1`; De Morgan `(x + y)′ = x′y′`, `(xy)′ = x′ + y′`; double negation `(x′)′ = x`; distribution both ways; **absorption** `x + xy = x`, `x(x + y) = x`; **combining the opposites** `xy + xy′ = x`, `(x + y)(x + y′) = x`. Handy consequence: `x + x′y = x + y`.

steps: `x′ + xy′ = x′ + y′` (the consequence `a + a′b = a + b` with `a = x′`).
So `xy + z(x′ + y′)`, and `x′ + y′ = (xy)′` by De Morgan.
`xy + (xy)′z = xy + z` (same consequence again, with `a = xy`).

tries.q: Simplify `a + ab′c`.
tries.why: Absorption: `x + x·(anything) = x`.

tries.q: Simplify `pq′ + pq`.
tries.why: Combining the opposites: `xy′ + xy = x`.

tries.q: Simplify `(m + n)′ + m`.
tries.why: De Morgan: `m′n′ + m`, then `m + m′n′ = m + n′`.

tries.q: Simplify `(u + v)(u + v′)(u′ + v)`.
tries.why: The first two combine to `u` (opposites). Then `u(u′ + v) = uu′ + uv = uv`.

trap.test: Try `x = 1, y = 0`: left side is 1, but `y` is 0.

blocks.magic: Absorb (`x + xy = x`), combine opposites (`xy + xy′ = x`), and `x + x′y = x + y`.

blocks.title: Building everything from one gate (NOR)
blocks.summary: With NOR alone you can make NOT, OR and AND, so any formula can be built from NOR gates only.
blocks.picture: A LEGO set with a single brick shape that can still build anything. Chip makers love this: one gate type is cheaper to manufacture.
blocks.official: `x NOR y` = `(x + y)′` (not-or). It can express every other operation: `x′ = x NOR x`; `x + y = (x NOR y) NOR (x NOR y)`; `x · y = (x NOR x) NOR (y NOR y)`. Since every formula uses only `′`, `+`, `·` (after removing `⇒`, `⇔`), every formula can be written with NOR alone. Problem set 2's challenge asks the same question for **nand**, `(x · y)′`: try it yourself with the same method.

watch.answer: **NOT from NOR:** feed the same input to both legs.

tries.q: Show `x + y = (x NOR y) NOR (x NOR y)`.
tries.a: `(x NOR y) NOR (x NOR y) = (x NOR y)′` (by the NOT trick) `= ((x + y)′)′ = x + y`.
tries.why: NOR then NOT gives OR.

tries.q: Show `x · y = (x NOR x) NOR (y NOR y)`.
tries.a: `= x′ NOR y′ = (x′ + y′)′ = x″y″ = xy` (De Morgan, double negation).
tries.why: Negate both inputs, then NOR: that's AND.

tries.q: Can every formula be written using only `+` and `′` (no `·`)?
tries.why: Replace every `·` this way.

trap.tempting: NOR can't make AND because it contains an OR.
trap.correct: Negating the inputs first turns the OR inside into an AND (De Morgan): `(x′ + y′)′ = xy`.
trap.test: Write the target with De Morgan until only `+` and `′` appear.

blocks.magic: `x′ = x NOR x`; OR = NOR then NOT; AND = NOR of the NOTs.

items.why: Bracket the product before negating it.
Complementation.
`+ 1` always gives 1.
Everything in `S` that isn't in `{p}`.
Combining the opposites (with `b` as the common part).
Absorption, the product version.
`x + x′y = x + y` with `x = a′`.
OR gives `(1, 1, 1)`; NOT gives `(0, 0, 0)`.

check.expr: tuple(1 - (a | b) for a, b in zip((1,1,0),(0,1,1)))

items.q: Translate `(p ⇒ q) ∧ r` into BA notation (remove `⇒` first).

blocks.sub: Exam style: find an optimal (shortest) equivalent expression, like the lecture's exercise 10.2.9. All expressions here are original.

items.q: Find the shortest expression equivalent to `x′yz + xyz + xy′z`.
items.why: `x′yz + xyz = yz` (opposites). Then `yz + xy′z = z(y + xy′) = z(y + x)`.

items.q: Find the shortest expression equivalent to `(a + b)′ + a′b + ab′`.
items.why: `(a + b)′ = a′b′`. Then `a′b′ + a′b = a′`. Then `a′ + ab′ = a′ + b′`.

items.q: Find the shortest expression equivalent to `pq + p′r + qr`.
items.why: `qr = qr(p + p′) = pqr + p′qr`, and each piece is absorbed by `pq` or `p′r`. (This is the *consensus* rule.)
De Morgan on each: `x′y″ + x″y′ = x′y + xy′`.

items.q: Which options are equivalent to `a + a′b`?
items.why: `a + a′b = a + b`. (3) is `(a′b′)′`, which is `a + b` by De Morgan. (1) drops `a`; (4) is AND.

items.q: Find the shortest expression equivalent to `(p + q)′ + r + p(qr + q′r′)′`.
items.why: `(p + q)′ = p′q′`. `(qr + q′r′)′` is "`q` and `r` differ" `= qr′ + q′r`, so the last term is `pqr′ + pq′r`. Now `pq′r` is absorbed by `r`, and `r + pqr′ = r + pq`.
`(b + c)′ = b′c′`. With `b = 0`, the first factor needs `a′`, i.e. `a = 0`. With `a = 0` and `c = 0`, the middle factor `a + c` is 0.

items.q: Is `T = {0, 1, 2}` with `x + y = max(x, y)`, `x · y = min(x, y)`, `x′ = 2 − x`, `0`, `1` := `0`, `2` a Boolean algebra?
items.a: **No.** It has 3 elements (not a power of 2), and complementation fails: `1 + 1′ = max(1, 1) = 1`, not the top element `2`.
items.why: Finite BAs have `2ᵏ` elements. The middle element has no proper complement.

check.expr: max(1, 2-1) != 2 and 3 not in [2**k for k in range(5)]

items.q: How many binary Boolean functions `f(x, y)` satisfy `f(0, 0) = 0`?
items.why: One of the 4 rows is fixed; the other 3 rows are free: `2³ = 8`.

check.expr: sum(1 for f in product([0,1], repeat=4) if f[0] == 0)

items.q: Show that every formula can be written with only `⇒` and `⊥`. (Hint: build `¬` and `∨` first.)
items.a: `¬p ≡ p ⇒ ⊥`. `p ∨ q ≡ ¬p ⇒ q ≡ (p ⇒ ⊥) ⇒ q`. With `¬` and `∨`, De Morgan gives `∧`: `p ∧ q ≡ ¬(¬p ∨ ¬q)`. So every formula can be rewritten.
items.why: Same method as the NOR idea: build NOT, then OR, then use De Morgan.

items.q: How many Boolean functions of 2 variables?

lines: BA examples: `{0, 1}`; bit vectors with bitwise ops; `Pow(S)` with `∪`, `∩`, complement; `Map(S, B)`.
Finite BAs have `2ᵏ` elements; same size ⇒ isomorphic (`Pow(S) ≃ B^|S|`).
Laws that shrink expressions: idempotence, complements, identity/annihilator, De Morgan, absorption, combining opposites.
NOR (or nand) alone can build every Boolean function.
